reason: Under 'Default certificate' the ALB guide says an HTTPS listener needs exactly one certificate, the default certificate; under 'Certificate list' it says the list supports multiple domains on one port with a certificate per domain, selected by an algorithm with SNI support.

The EventBridge page states daily expiration events for all active certificates, 45 days before for private/imported and 30 days before for public, and that PutAccountConfiguration changes the timing.

The Aug 13, 2026 What's New post says existing public certificates can now switch from email to DNS without reissue or ARN change, with up to 72 hours to add the CNAME records; the guide note states the earlier rule (cannot switch, delete and request again); the 2027 phase-out is quoted.

The Jun 17, 2025 post introduces exportable public certificates for EC2 instances, containers or on-premises hosts and says previously ACM public certificates could only be used with integrated AWS services; the doc history row confirms the date.

The Feb 18, 2026 post states a maximum validity of 198 days compared to the previous 395 days, that all new and renewed public certificates get 198 days, that existing 395-day certificates stay valid until renewal or expiry, and that no customer action is required.

Under 'AWS CloudFormation' the best-practices page recommends not creating a separate certificate per test environment because it exhausts the quota, and creating a wildcard certificate covering the test domain names instead (the example says 'a single wildcard certificate').

The DNS validation page says non-Route 53 users must manually enter the ACM CNAME records into the provider's database; the domain validation page says that if you can't edit the DNS database you must use email validation.
The exportable certificates page says they can be deployed anywhere including EC2 instances, containers and on-premises hosts, extending ACM public certificates beyond integrated AWS services.

Under 'Limitations' the guide says you must manage the deployment of exported certificates; the 'How it works' list says ACM manages renewals and sends notifications; the integrated-services page names AWS Workload Credentials Provider for automating exportable certificates.

The FAQ says ACM continues to support email validation for customers who can't change DNS; the Aug 2026 post gives the March 31 2027 end of issuance and September 30 2027 end of renewal for email-validated certificates.

The FAQ gives 198 days for public certificates and any validity period for private certificates issued directly from a private CA without ACM management; the ACME page gives 45 days for ACME-issued certificates, shorter than other ACM public certificates.

The pricing table rows give $7.00 per FQDN and $79.00 per wildcard name, charged at issuance and again only on renewal; the FAQ states the reduction from $15 and $149 with the move from 395 to 198 days; the 10,000 free API calls tier is quoted.
The Feb 18, 2026 doc history row of the ACM guide says public certificates are now 198 days and 'Private certificates remain valid for 13 months (395 days)'.
The private certificates page says ACM can request a certificate if you have access to an existing private CA created by AWS Private CA, in your account or shared by a different account.

The FAQ lists both options: full automation of renewal and deployment for private certificates used with integrated services such as ELB and API Gateway while the issuing CA is Active, and automatic renewal with customer retrieval and deployment for exported private certificates.

The Feb 18, 2026 doc history row and post say public certificates now renew 45 days before expiry and existing older-validity certificates renew 60 days before expiry; the DNS and email renewal conditions are quoted.

The characteristics page says ACM certificates are valid for 198 days; the Feb 18, 2026 doc history row says reduced from 13 months (395 days); the ACME page gives 45 days for ACME-issued certificates.

The General Reference quota row gives 2,500 ACM certificates per Region, adjustable Yes, counting PENDING or ISSUED; the ACM quotas page gives 2500 and the exclusions and expired/revoked note quoted in the condition.

The managed renewal page lists ELIGIBLE if associated with another AWS service or exported since issue or last renewal, and NOT ELIGIBLE if issued via Private CA IssueCertificate, imported or already expired; the Note excludes ACME certificates.
The Parameter Store reference says, with one exception, no validation is performed on the value; for String parameters with data type aws:ec2:image it validates the AMI format.
The events page says EventBridge and SNS can notify about parameter changes on a best effort basis, including parameter or label version create/update/delete and parameter policy changes or status.

The Lambda extension page says cached values are used until the TTL (SSM_PARAMETER_STORE_TTL) expires and then the value is retrieved from Parameter Store again, and that the extension uses the function's own credentials, so its IAM role needs Parameter Store permissions.
The policies page says parameter policies are available for advanced-tier parameters; the tier table row shows Parameter policies: Standard 'Not supported', Advanced 'Supported'.

The KMS page says KMS keys encrypt SecureString values on create or change and decrypt on access; under both the standard and advanced sections the default is the AWS managed key aws/ssm, and a customer managed key can be used.
The default tier page says standard parameters are available at no cost with size and feature restrictions and the advanced tier offers higher limits and extra features at a cost.

The Parameter Store features Note states the claim verbatim: update takes effect on next read without validation, gradual rollout or automatic revert, and AWS AppConfig adds a managed deployment workflow.

The Encryption row of the comparison table (header Feature | Parameter Store | AWS AppConfig | AWS Secrets Manager) gives 'Optional with SecureString and AWS KMS' for Parameter Store and 'AWS KMS encryption at rest with an AWS managed or customer managed key' for Secrets Manager.
The Parameter Store overview defines it as a centralized configuration data store for named values called parameters, with the same examples of parameter data.
The KMS page says a SecureString value is returned encrypted, and setting WithDecryption to true on GetParameter makes Parameter Store call KMS Decrypt on your behalf and return a plaintext value.

The Important box on the resource-based policies page says validation and BlockPublicPolicy prevent public access through policies attached directly to secrets, and to also inspect identity-based policies of principals such as IAM roles and resource policies of resources such as KMS keys.
The Python caching component page says the cache refreshes secrets every hour by default and the refresh frequency is configurable; scope is limited to the Python component as claimed.

The Mar 4, 2025 post gives DescribeSecret 40,000 requests per second, matching the current quota row; in the saved What's New feed the 'increased to 10,000 requests per second' sentence sits in the 2022-11-11 item, so it is the earlier increase.

In the saved What's New feed the 'at least 99.99%' sentence belongs to the 2023-12-05 item 'AWS Secrets Manager announces 99.99% Service Level Agreement' (an updated SLA) and the 'at least 99.9%' sentence to the 2019-01-17 SLA item, so the claimed order and per-Region, per-month scope hold.

The dynamic references page says they specify external values stored in other services and decouple sensitive information from templates, are retrieved during stack and change set operations, and names Parameter Store secure strings and Secrets Manager secrets.
The page says AWS Config rules evaluate whether secrets rotate in compliance with your standards and identify non-conforming secrets, and that data can be aggregated across accounts and Regions.

The delete page says secrets are not deleted immediately but made inaccessible at once and scheduled for deletion after a recovery window; the CLI example deletes a secret immediately without a recovery window and it can't be recovered.
The ECS guide paragraph states the claim verbatim and the claim attributes it to the ECS guide.

The encryption page says Secrets Manager does not use the KMS key to encrypt the value directly, uses it to generate and encrypt a data key that encrypts the value, and requests a new data key whenever the value changes.

The FAQ Rotation answer gives, as an example for database secrets, use of admin credentials provided by you to create a clone user with the same privileges and a different password; the claim keeps the 'example' framing.

The managed rotation page says the service configures and manages rotation and you don't use a Lambda function to update the secret and database credentials; RDS is listed for master user credentials, as in the condition.
